q: A torch bulb, an ideal diode and a battery are connected in series. The bulb glows. The battery is now turned round, with nothing else changed. The bulb:
o: Does not glow, because the diode is now reverse biased
x: Reversing the battery reverse biases the diode, which then allows almost no current, so the bulb goes out. A diode conducts in one direction only; alternate half-cycles would need an AC supply.

q: A good p-n junction diode is tested with an ohmmeter, first with the leads one way round and then reversed. The two readings should be:
o: A low resistance one way and a very high resistance the other way
x: Forward biased, the junction has a low resistance; reverse biased, it has a very high resistance. Low both ways means a short-circuited diode, and very high both ways means an open-circuited one.

q: A silicon diode (forward voltage drop 0.7 V) is connected in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5.7 V battery so that the diode is forward biased. The current in the circuit is:
x: The resistor gets 5.7 − 0.7 = 5.0 V, so I = 5.0 V / 1000 Ω = 5 mA. Ignoring the diode's drop gives 5.7 mA; adding it instead of subtracting gives 6.4 mA.

q: A half-wave rectifier uses one silicon diode (forward drop 0.7 V). The AC input to the diode has a peak value of 10 V. The peak voltage across the load resistor is about:
x: At the peak the diode conducts and drops 0.7 V, so the load gets 10 − 0.7 = 9.3 V. Ignoring the drop gives 10 V; adding it gives 10.7 V; 7.1 V is the rms value of a 10 V peak, not the peak output.

q: A bridge rectifier made of four silicon diodes (forward drop 0.7 V each) is fed from a transformer whose secondary voltage has a peak of 12 V. The peak voltage across the load is about:
x: In a bridge, two diodes conduct in series with the load in each half-cycle, so the peak load voltage is 12 − 2 × 0.7 = 10.6 V. Counting only one diode gives 11.3 V; counting all four gives 9.2 V.

q: A capacitor of large capacitance is connected in parallel with the load resistor of a full-wave rectifier. The purpose of the capacitor is to:
o: Smooth the output by charging at the peaks and discharging between them
Double the frequency of the output
Block the direct current from reaching the load
Convert the output back into alternating current
x: The capacitor charges to near the peak voltage and then supplies the load while the rectified voltage falls, so the ripple is reduced and the output is nearly steady DC. It does not change the pulse frequency, and in parallel it does not block DC from the load.

q: The small current that flows through a reverse-biased p-n junction is carried mainly by:
o: Majority carriers: holes in the p-region and electrons in the n-region
The fixed ions in the depletion region
Minority carriers: holes in the n-region and electrons in the p-region
x: Reverse bias stops the majority carriers, but the junction field sweeps across the few thermally produced minority carriers, giving a tiny reverse current. Fixed ions cannot move, so they carry no current.

q: A p-n junction is kept at a fixed reverse bias, well below breakdown, while its temperature is raised. Its reverse current:
o: Decreases, because the depletion region becomes wider
Stays exactly the same, as it depends only on the voltage
Increases, because more minority carriers are produced thermally
x: The reverse current is due to minority carriers, which are created by thermal breaking of bonds; heating produces more of them, so the reverse current rises. A fixed bias does not widen the depletion region further, so the current does not fall.

q: A germanium diode and a silicon diode are each forward biased with a slowly rising voltage. Compared with the silicon diode, the germanium diode starts to conduct appreciably at:
x: The potential barrier of a germanium junction is about 0.3 V, compared with about 0.7 V for silicon, so germanium conducts at a lower forward voltage. 0.7 V is the silicon value.

q: A 9 V battery is connected across two parallel branches. Branch 1 is a 1 kΩ resistor in series with an ideal diode that is forward biased. Branch 2 is another 1 kΩ resistor in series with an ideal diode that is reverse biased. The current drawn from the battery is:
x: The forward-biased ideal diode acts as a closed switch, so branch 1 carries 9 V / 1 kΩ = 9 mA; the reverse-biased diode acts as an open switch, so branch 2 carries nothing. Total = 9 mA. Letting both branches conduct gives 18 mA.

q: The reverse voltage across an ordinary p-n junction is slowly increased. When it reaches the breakdown voltage:
o: The reverse current falls to zero
x: At breakdown the strong junction field frees large numbers of carriers (avalanche or Zener breakdown), so the reverse current increases suddenly and can destroy an ordinary diode. Below breakdown the reverse current stays small and nearly constant.

q: A full-wave rectifier is connected to the 50 Hz mains. The time from the start of one output pulse to the start of the next is:
x: One input cycle lasts 1/50 s = 20 ms, and a full-wave rectifier gives two output pulses per cycle, so one pulse starts every 10 ms (100 pulses per second). 20 ms is the spacing for a half-wave rectifier.

q: A photovoltaic (solar) cell:
o: Emits light when a current is passed through it
Needs a reverse-bias battery to produce a current
Converts light energy directly into electrical energy without any external bias
x: Light makes electron-hole pairs at the junction, and the junction's own field separates them, so the cell itself acts as a source of e.m.f. Emitting light is what an LED does; a photodiode, not a solar cell, is used with reverse bias.

q: LEDs that give red, yellow and green light are made from different semiconductor compounds. The colour of the light from an LED depends mainly on:
o: The energy gap of the semiconductor material
The size of the current through it
The value of the series resistor
x: Each photon is emitted when an electron falls across the energy gap, so the photon energy, and hence its wavelength and colour, is set by the gap of the material (a larger gap gives a shorter wavelength). The current only changes the brightness.

q: Which statement about how an LED, a photodiode used as a light detector and a photovoltaic cell are operated is correct?
o: The LED is reverse biased, the photodiode is forward biased and the photovoltaic cell is reverse biased
The LED is forward biased, the photodiode is reverse biased and the photovoltaic cell needs no bias
x: An LED needs forward bias so that electrons and holes recombine and emit light. A photodiode works in reverse bias, where its small reverse current rises with light intensity. A photovoltaic cell produces its own e.m.f. from light, so it is used without an external bias.

q: In an NPN transistor, the middle region, which is very thin and lightly doped, is the:
x: The base is the thin, lightly doped middle layer, so most charge carriers from the emitter pass through it to the collector and the base current is small. The emitter is heavily doped and the collector is the largest region.

q: A transistor is used as a switch in a circuit. It acts as an open (OFF) switch when:
o: The base current is large, so the collector current is at its maximum
The base current is zero, so the collector current is almost zero
The collector-emitter voltage is almost zero
The base-emitter junction is forward biased with a large current
x: With no base current the transistor is cut off: I_C ≈ 0 and almost the whole supply voltage appears across the collector and emitter, like an open switch. A large base current saturates it, with V_CE near zero, which is the ON state.

q: A transistor with current gain β = 80 has a 2 kΩ resistor in its collector circuit. The base current increases by 50 μA. The increase in the voltage across the collector resistor is:
x: ΔI_C = β ΔI_B = 80 × 50 μA = 4 mA, so ΔV = ΔI_C × R = 4 × 10⁻³ × 2000 = 8 V. Forgetting the gain gives 50 μA × 2 kΩ = 0.1 V; a prefix slip (2 kΩ taken as 200 Ω) gives 0.8 V.

q: An ideal operational amplifier has an input resistance that is:
o: Zero, so it draws a very large current
Infinitely large, so it draws no current from the input
x: An ideal op-amp has infinite input resistance, infinite open-loop gain and zero output resistance; the infinite input resistance means its inputs draw no current. This is why the current through the input resistor all flows through the feedback resistor.

q: A non-inverting amplifier has a 1 kΩ resistor between the inverting input and earth. For a voltage gain of 11, the feedback resistor must be:
x: For a non-inverting amplifier, gain = 1 + R₂/R₁, so 11 = 1 + R₂/1 kΩ and R₂ = 10 kΩ. Using the inverting formula R₂/R₁ = 11 gives 11 kΩ.

q: An inverting amplifier has an input resistor of 1 kΩ and a feedback resistor of 20 kΩ. The op-amp is powered from a ±9 V supply. A steady input of +1 V is applied. The output voltage is about:
x: The ideal formula gives V_out = −(20/1) × 1 = −20 V, but the output cannot go beyond the supply voltages, so the op-amp saturates at about −9 V. Using the formula without the supply limit gives −20 V; using 1 + R₂/R₁ gives −21 V.

q: For a two-input logic gate, the output is 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 for every other input combination. The gate is:
x: NAND is AND followed by NOT: AND gives 1 only for inputs 1, 1, so NAND gives 0 only for inputs 1, 1. AND has the opposite outputs; NOR gives 1 only for inputs 0, 0.

q: Inputs P and Q are fed to an AND gate, and its output is passed through a NOT gate. The final output is 0 for:
o: P = 1, Q = 0 and P = 0, Q = 1 only
Every combination of P and Q
x: The final output is NOT(P·Q), the NAND function. P·Q = 1 only when both inputs are 1, so the final output is 0 only for P = 1, Q = 1. P = 0, Q = 0 is the only zero of an OR gate, not of this circuit.

q: Inputs P and Q are fed to a NOR gate. The output of this gate is fed to both inputs of a second NOR gate, whose two inputs are joined together. The final output is the same as that of:
o: An OR gate with inputs P and Q
An AND gate with inputs P and Q
A NOR gate with inputs P and Q
A NAND gate with inputs P and Q
x: The first gate gives NOT(P + Q). A NOR gate with joined inputs acts as a NOT gate, so the second gate inverts this to P + Q, the OR function. Check: P = Q = 0 gives 1 then 0, and any input 1 gives 0 then 1. Forgetting the second inversion leaves NOR.
